text: If I get the offer in March, I will accept it the same week.
If the tuition were free, I would go tomorrow.
If I miss the deadline, there will not be a second chance this year.
If I had another year, I would apply to six places instead of two.
If I get the offer in March, I will send the certificate the same week.
If I were you, I would find out what the number covers before you answer.
And you, what would you do if the answer arrived tomorrow?

The question I get every October is which university, and the question nobody asks me is how many. That second one is the one that decides the year, so let me start there. If a family applies to one or two places, they are betting twelve months on two answers, and if both of them come back no in April, there is genuinely nothing left to do until the following September. Now, a list has three parts and they are not the same size. One or two long shots, where you are below what the university normally takes and you send it anyway. Three or four matches, where you meet what the page asks for and it could honestly go either way. And at least one that is close to certain and affordable without any scholarship at all, because if every place on your list depends on money you do not have yet, that is not a list. And the last thing, which is the one I actually came here to say. In fifteen years the thing students regret is never the application that failed. It is the one they did not send, and it is always the long shot, and the reason is always the same sentence: I would not have got in anyway. Nobody knows that. If you would regret not sending it, send it.

I turned down a place at a university everybody in my school had heard of, with a partial scholarship, and for about two months people assumed I had been scared, or that my parents had said no. Neither of those is what happened. The scholarship covered the tuition and it covered nothing else, and the city it was in is one of the most expensive in the country. If I had taken it, I would have been working four evenings and a Saturday, and studying with whatever was left, and that is not the year I went there for. So I said no, and I said it early, which I think matters. What I would do differently is the list. Two applications is not a list, it is a coin, and I knew that in October and did it anyway. If I had sent five, I would have had something to compare. But the decision itself I would make again tomorrow with the same information, and I have stopped apologising for it in conversations.
If I get the offer in March, I will accept it the same week.
If I miss the deadline, there will not be a second chance this year.
If I had another year, I would apply to six places instead of two.
If the tuition were free, I would go tomorrow.
If I were you, I would send both applications.
If the scholarship does not arrive in April, I will use the backup plan.
If I get the offer in March, I will send the certificate the same week.
If I were you, I would find out what the number covers before you answer.
And you, what would you do if the answer arrived tomorrow?
